title: CASE OF A.Ö. AND H.Ö. v. ROMANIA
conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect)
summary: In A.Ö. and H.Ö. v. Romania, the applicants were two sisters, with the first applicant, A.Ö., described in the judgment as a woman of Roma ethnic origin. The case focused on the vulnerability of a Roma minor in state care who alleged sexual abuse and the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation. In 2018, while living in a care home in Romania, A.Ö. reported being sexually abused by an older man. Despite her age and vulnerable status, the investigation by Romanian authorities was marred by significant shortcomings: officials mistakenly recorded her age, relied solely on the suspect’s statements, failed to assess her capacity to consent, and allowed harmful stereotypes—such as blaming the minor for provoking the abuse—to influence their approach. Additionally, A.Ö. was represented by an employee of the care home (against which complaints had been made) and an ex officio lawyer, neither of whom took meaningful action on her behalf. The European Court of Human Rights found that these failures amounted to a violation of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically the procedural obligation to conduct an effective investigation into inhuman and degrading treatment. The Court awarded A.Ö. €12,500 in non-pecuniary damages. The judgment highlighted the persistent problem of inadequate responses to gender-based violence against Roma women and girls in Europe.
